title: Methods and Sorting
summary: You will learn how Java methods (Methoden) use parameters (Parameter), return values (Rückgaben), and arrays (Arrays). Insertion sort (Insertion Sort) builds a sorted prefix (sortiertes Präfix) by inserting each new element. Reference copies (Referenzkopien), condition order (Reihenfolge der Bedingungen), stability (Stabilität), and quadratic cost (quadratische Kosten) are key points.
concepts: Local variable and precondition (Lokale Variable und Vorbedingung)
Array reference and aliasing (Array-Referenz und Aliasing)
Mutation and independent copy (Mutation und echte Kopie)
keyFacts: A method is a named, reusable block of code that encapsulates tasks and breaks problems down.
A formal parameter (formaler Parameter) appears in a method definition; an actual argument (aktuelles Argument) is the concrete value supplied when the method is called.
A void method (void-Methode) returns no value and is also called a procedure (Prozedur).
A precondition must hold before a call; min requires a nonempty array because it reads b[0].
The words after the class name are passed as strings to main(String[] args).
In an assignment such as int result = min(a), result is initialized only after min returns.
Java copies each argument value when a method is called: it copies the value for a primitive type and the reference for an array.
A method can change the shared array with b[0] = 9; by contrast, b = new int[2] only reassigns the local reference.
When two variables point to the same array, they alias each other; a separate copy requires a new array and copying its elements.
Insertion sort builds a sorted prefix step by step and returns a sorted copy of the input.
locate finds the insertion position; shift copies the affected elements to the right, after which x is written at position j.
shift runs from right to left so that values are not overwritten before they are copied.
In j < i && x >= b[j], if the left-hand part is false, the right-hand part is not evaluated; this prevents b[i] from being read.
With x >= b[j], locate advances past equal elements, so the new element is placed after them and the sort remains stable.
In iteration i, locate and shift together take about i steps; overall, 1 + 2 + … + (n − 1) = n(n − 1)/2 ∈ Θ(n²).
After a[i] is inserted, b[0..i] is sorted and contains exactly the first i + 1 input values.

review.notes: Geprüft: 44 Fragen. Ergänzt wurde beim Boss-Sortierbeispiel der fehlende Algorithmus im Kontext, damit die Instanz ohne Vorlesung lösbar ist. Antworten, Distraktoren, Erklärungen, Mermaid-Diagramme und verify-Skripte geprüft.

questions.prompt: What is a method in Java?

options.text: A variable that exists only in main
An expression that always returns a value
An array with a fixed length
A named, reusable block of code

questions.explanation: A method groups statements under a name. It can be reused and helps break a problem into subtasks.

questions.prompt: In `public static int min(int[] b)`, `b` is a ___.

options.text: return value
command-line argument
actual argument
formal parameter

questions.explanation: A formal parameter is the input variable in a method definition. An actual argument would be the concrete value supplied when the method is called, such as `a` in `min(a)`.

questions.prompt: A `return` statement ends the current method call and can return a value.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: `return result;` ends the call and returns `result` to the calling location.

questions.prompt: Which statements describe advantages of methods? More than one answer may be correct.

options.text: A problem can be broken down into smaller subtasks.
Every method must return an array.
A block of code written once can be called repeatedly.
Several steps are given a name.

questions.explanation: Methods encapsulate tasks, enable reuse, and support breaking a problem down. A return type can also be `void`.

questions.prompt: What is a method with return type `void` also called?

options.text: Invariant
Procedure
Constructor
Actual argument

questions.explanation: A `void` method returns no value and is also called a procedure.

options.text: Hel lo World!
HelloWorld!
World!loHel
TestHelloWorld!

questions.explanation: `args[0]`, `args[1]`, and `args[2]` are the strings `Hel`, `lo`, and `World!`. Concatenation joins them without adding spaces.

questions.prompt: In the diagram, `main` waits while `min(a)` is running. What does the return arrow from `min` mean?

context.content:
flowchart LR
  M["main: int result = min(a)"] -. "call" .-> F["min: Werte prüfen"]
  F --> R["return result"]
  R -. "return" .-> W["main: result setzen, dann write"]
context.caption: Call and return between main and min

options.text: `min` is started again without arguments.
The local variable in `min` becomes a local variable in `main`.
Execution jumps back to the beginning of the program.
The return value goes back to the waiting call in `main`.

questions.explanation: After `return result`, execution returns to the waiting method call. There, `main` can use the return value.

questions.prompt: The method `min(int[] b)` begins with `int result = b[0];`. What precondition does it need for this access to be valid?

options.text: The array must contain exactly two elements.
All elements must be positive.
The array must already be sorted.
The array must contain at least one element.

questions.explanation: An empty array has no element at index 0. The array must therefore be nonempty for this access.

questions.prompt: A local variable named `result` in `main` and a local variable named `result` in `min` are the same variable.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: Local variables are scoped to their respective blocks. The same name in two methods does not make them the same variable.

questions.prompt: Which statements about `main(String[] args)` are correct? More than one answer may be correct.

options.text: `args[0]` always contains the class name.
Words after the class name are stored as strings in `args`.
`main` is the program's entry point.
`args` contains only numbers.

questions.explanation: `main` is the program entry point. The words supplied after the class name when the program starts are stored as strings in `args`.

questions.prompt: In the method header `public static int[] readArray(int number)`, `int[]` is the ___.

options.text: return type
body
method name
formal parameters

questions.explanation: The return type specifies what type the method returns. Here, it is an array of `int` values.

options.text: The call causes an error.
There is no output.

questions.explanation: `zero` receives a copy of the `int` value. The assignment `number = 0` changes this local copy, while `n` retains the value 2.

questions.explanation: The argument value is a reference to the same array. `b[0] = 9` mutates this shared array, so `a[0]` is 9 afterward.

questions.prompt: Given `int[] a = {4, 8}; min(a);`, what is the actual argument in the call `min(a)`?

options.text: The concrete value that `a` refers to
The formal parameter `b`
The method body of `min`
The return type `int`

questions.explanation: The actual argument is the concrete value passed when the method is called. Here, it is the array reference stored in `a`.

questions.prompt: For `locate(b, x, i)`, `j` starts at 0 and is incremented while `j < i && x >= b[j]` is true. For `b = [1, 4, 8, 10]`, `x = 6`, and `i = 4`, what index does `locate` return?
questions.explanation: `6 >= 1` and `6 >= 4` are true, so `j` reaches 2. There, `6 >= 8` is false, so 2 is returned.

questions.prompt: For `shift(b, j, i)`, `b[k + 1] = b[k]` is executed as `k` runs down from `i - 1` to `j`. How many assignments are made when `j = 2` and `i = 5`?
questions.explanation: `k` takes the values 4, 3, and 2. The assignment is therefore executed exactly three times.

questions.prompt: In the process, `j < i` is true, but `x >= b[j]` is false. Which step is executed next?

context.caption: Find the position, shift elements, and insert the value

options.text: `return j`

questions.explanation: The loop condition is false overall because the comparison with `b[j]` fails. The process exits `locate` and then begins shifting with `k = i - 1`.

questions.prompt: Which statements about `int[] b = a` are correct? More than one answer may be correct.

options.text: `a` and `b` then refer to the same array.
The assignment copies all array elements into a new array.
A change to `b[0]` is also visible through `a[0]`.
`a` is automatically redirected to a new array.

questions.explanation: The assignment copies the reference, not the array. Both variables therefore point to the same elements.

questions.prompt: In `insert`, the steps are performed in this order: `locate`, `shift`, then `___`.

options.text: `b = new int[i]`
`return b[j]`

questions.explanation: First, the insertion position is found; then elements are shifted to the right. Finally, `x` is placed at the freed position `j`.

questions.prompt: If `copy(a)` creates and returns a new array with the same elements, later changes to this new array do not automatically change `a`.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: A true copy is a separate array. Unlike a simple reference assignment, the two variables do not share the same array.

questions.prompt: When sorting the input `{8, 3, 6}`, what is the sorted prefix in the result array `b` after the first element has been inserted?

options.text: The prefix is empty until all values have been inserted.

questions.explanation: After the first iteration, only `a[0]`, which is 8, has been inserted. A single element already forms a sorted prefix.

questions.prompt: Why is the index check on the left in `while (j < i && x >= b[j])`? More than one answer may be correct.

options.text: Swapping the order would be equally safe for every possible array and every `i`.
If `j < i` is false, short-circuit evaluation prevents `b[j]` from being read.
The order ensures that `b[j]` always takes the value `x`.
This skips the right-hand part of the condition when `j = i`.

questions.explanation: With `&&`, the right-hand part is checked only if the left-hand part is true. Thus, when `j = i`, `j < i` prevents access to `b[j]`.

questions.prompt: With `locate` using the condition `x >= b[j]`, `j` moves past equal values. As a result, a new element of the same size is inserted after them.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: The `>=` comparison lets the search continue even when values are equal. The new element is placed after the existing equal values, preserving their order.

questions.prompt: When shifting `[1, 3, 7, 9, 0]` to make an insertion starting at `j = 2`, why does `shift` run from right to left?

options.text: So that each value is copied before its position is overwritten.
So that the array gets a new length.
So that `j` increases automatically during the shift.
So that the values are sorted in descending order in the result.

questions.explanation: Going from right to left preserves each value until it has been copied. If shifting from left to right, for example, 9 would be overwritten before it was copied.

source.heading: Warum von rechts nach links schieben?

questions.prompt: An array with $n=6$ values is built using the described insertion sort variant. Insertions are made at indices $i=1,2,3,4,5$. In this cost model, the insertion at index $i$ takes exactly $i$ steps. How many steps are there in total?
questions.explanation: The insertions take $1+2+3+4+5=15$ steps.
First 4 is inserted, then 1 is placed before it, and finally 3 is inserted between 1 and 4. The result array therefore contains 1, 3, 4.

questions.prompt: What does the invariant assert after inserting `a[i]`?

options.text: `b` is fully sorted after every iteration.
`b[i..n-1]` is sorted and contains all input values.
`b[0..i]` is sorted and contains exactly the first `i + 1` input values.
`b[0..i]` contains only values greater than `a[i]`.

questions.explanation: After each iteration, the leading section up to index `i` forms a sorted prefix. It contains exactly the input values processed through `a[i]`.

questions.prompt: Which statement is supported by the process after each iteration?

context.content:
flowchart LR
  A["Vor Iteration i: b[0..i-1] sortiert"] --> B["a[i] passend einfügen"]
  B --> C["Danach: b[0..i] sortiert"]
  C --> D{"i = n - 1?"}
  D -- "nein" --> A
  D -- "ja" --> E["b ist sortierte Kopie von a"]
context.caption: The invariant across iterations

options.text: Before the first iteration, the entire result array is sorted and filled.
At `i = n - 1`, `b` contains only the last input element.
After the iteration for `i`, `b[0..i]` is sorted.
The method sorts the input by directly changing `a`.

questions.explanation: Each step inserts `a[i]` into the appropriate position in the prefix that is already sorted. After the final insertion, the entire array `b` is therefore sorted.

questions.prompt: Suppose `b` has length 3 and a modified loop condition is `x >= b[j] && j < i`. If `j = i = 3` is reached, which access is attempted first?

options.text: First, `b[3]` is read; this index is outside an array of length 3.
First, `j < i` is checked and the array access is skipped.
The condition is treated as true without evaluating either part.
The value `x` is written to `b[3]`.

questions.explanation: With `&&`, evaluation proceeds from left to right. In the reversed order, `x >= b[j]` comes first; when `j = 3`, this accesses invalid index 3.

questions.prompt: Which statements about the cost of iteration `i` are correct? More than one answer may be correct.

options.text: Together, they always take `i²` steps.
The input determines whether `j` cancels out of the sum.
`locate` takes about `j` steps and `shift` takes exactly `i - j` steps.
Together, they take about `i` steps, independent of `j`.

questions.explanation: The substeps add up to `j + (i - j) = i`. The `j` terms cancel, so this estimate does not depend on the input.

questions.prompt: This variant still takes Θ(n²) time even on an already sorted input, because `locate` searches through the prefix from the left in every iteration.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: Even for sorted input, `locate` runs from index 0 to near `i`. The sum of these search lengths grows quadratically.

questions.prompt: According to the lecture notes, what does inlining a method call mean?

options.text: The JVM can automatically replace the call with the method body.
The method is always converted into an array.
The compiler deletes all local variables.
The caller terminates after the call.

questions.explanation: Inlining means replacing a call with the method body. The JVM can perform this transformation automatically.

questions.prompt: A route-selection program considers routes in the order A, B, C. A takes 7 minutes and has no stairs; B takes 5 minutes and has no stairs; C also takes 5 minutes and has no stairs. The rule selects the fastest route without stairs; if two routes take the same time, the one selected first remains selected. Which route is chosen?

options.text: No suitable route
B, because it is the first fastest route
A, because it comes first
C, because a tie favors the later route

questions.explanation: A is selected first, then replaced by the faster route B. C is not faster than B, so B remains selected in the tie.
`b = a` copies the reference, so both variables point to the same array. The change through `b[1]` is therefore visible when reading `a[1]`.

options.text: Accessing `b[0]` throws an exception.
There is no output.
false
true

questions.explanation: `b.length` is 0, so `j < b.length` is false. Short-circuit evaluation prevents `b[j]` from being read, and `safe` remains `false`.
`x[0] = y` first changes the shared array. `y = 100` changes only the local copy; after `x` is reassigned, `x[1] = 50` affects only the new array.

questions.prompt: The approximate step count for this sorting variant is $T(n)=\frac{n(n-1)}{2}$. How many steps does it take for $n=1000$?
questions.explanation: $1000\cdot999/2=499\,500$. The leading quadratic term explains the growth in Θ(n²).

questions.prompt: Which statements about sorting with helper methods are correct? More than one answer may be correct.

options.text: `insert` changes array `b` even though it does not return a value.
`sort` creates `b` and calls `insert` for each input element.
`locate` shifts the elements to the right.
`shift` finds the insertion position.

questions.explanation: `sort` creates the result array and inserts the values one by one. `insert` mutates the shared array; `locate` finds the position, while `shift` moves the elements.

questions.prompt: What result follows from the final path in the diagram if processing continues through `i = n - 1`?

context.content:
flowchart LR
  A["Vor Iteration i: b[0..i-1] sortiert"] --> B["a[i] passend einfügen"]
  B --> C["Danach: b[0..i] sortiert"]
  C --> D{"i = n - 1?"}
  D -- "nein" --> A
  D -- "ja" --> E["b ist sortierte Kopie von a"]
context.caption: From the sorted prefix to the complete result

options.text: `b` contains only a sorted prefix, with no remaining values.
`a` has been completely overwritten and contains only the last element.
`b` is a sorted copy of `a`.
`b` contains the values in reverse order.

questions.explanation: After each insertion, the prefix through `i` is sorted. When `i` reaches the last index, this prefix covers the entire result array and contains all the input values.

questions.prompt: Run insertion sort with `locate` and `shift` on `a = [17, 3, -2, 9, 0, 1, 7, 42, 5]`. What values does the returned array contain in ascending order?

context.caption: Algorithm for inserting into a sorted prefix

questions.explanation: Each element is inserted into the sorted prefix. All nine input values are preserved, giving `-2, 0, 1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 17, 42` in ascending order.

questions.prompt: Consider `int result = min(a); write(result);`. `min` computes its own local `result` internally and returns it with `return result`. When is the local value in `main` assigned?

options.text: Only after `min` has returned.
On each loop iteration of `min`, directly in `main`.
It is never assigned because `min` has a local variable.
Before the call to `min`.

questions.explanation: While `min` is running, `main` waits at the call site. Only afterward does the return value initialize `result` in `main`; the two local variables are distinct.

questions.prompt: A method receives `int[] x` and `int y`. It executes `x[0] = y; y = 100; x = new int[1];`. The caller had `a = {7}` and `v = 3`. What is true after the call? More than one answer may be correct.

options.text: `a` now refers to the method's new array.
`v` is 3.

questions.explanation: `x[0] = y` changes the shared array using the copied value 3. The change to `y` affects only the local copy, and reassigning `x` does not change `a`.

questions.prompt: `insert` can change the result array without returning a value because the copied parameter `b` still refers to the same array as in the caller.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: A return value is not needed: `b` contains a copy of the reference, allowing the method to change the shared array elements.

levels.title: In Practice: Sorting Tricks for Everyday Life

questions.prompt: Three views in a campus app need to use the same sequence of steps to display a place name consistently. Which solution uses methods effectively?

options.text: Create a separate copy of the entire place-data array in each view.
Pass the place name to the app as a command-line argument.
Sort the views by place name to make the code reusable.
Group the steps in a named method once and call it from all three views.

questions.explanation: A method groups a task under a name and can be reused in multiple places. This helps keep the views consistent.

questions.prompt: You start a Java tool in the terminal and want to pass it a file name and an option. Where do the words after the class name go in `main(String[] args)`?

options.text: As elements of the array `args`.
As the return value of `main`.
As local variables in every method that is called.
As elements of an automatically sorted array.

questions.explanation: Java passes the words after the class name as strings in the array `args`. The tool can interpret them as, for example, a file name and an option.

questions.prompt: Use this cost model for insertion sort: for `n` values, the work for `locate` and `shift` together takes `1 + 2 + … + (n − 1)` steps. How many steps does it take for 40 values?
questions.explanation: The sum is $1 + 2 + \dots + 39 = \frac{40 \cdot 39}{2} = 780$ steps.

questions.prompt: A Java app stores seats in a `boolean[]`. A method receives this array and sets `b[4] = true`; the array has at least five elements. What does the calling app see after the method call?

options.text: The method automatically works on a complete copy of the array.
The app's reference is set to a new array.
Its array also has the value `true` at index 4.
Only the local variable `b` changes; the app's array stays the same.

questions.explanation: The array reference is copied when the method is called; both variables still point to the same array. A change to an element is therefore also visible to the app.

questions.prompt: A timetable app initially displays connections in input order, then sorts them by departure minute. A stable sort keeps entries with the same sort key in their previous order. What happens to two connections with the same departure minute?

options.text: They are always ordered alphabetically by destination.
The connection that appeared later in the input always comes first.
One of the two connections is removed.
Their previous order is preserved.

questions.explanation: Stability preserves the order of equal sort keys. Thus, connections with the same departure minute keep their previous order.

questions.prompt: Using the same cost model, the work for `n` values is `1 + 2 + … + (n − 1)`. By what factor does the work increase from 20 to 40 values, rounded to one decimal place?
questions.explanation: For 20 values, it takes $190$ steps; for 40 values, $780$. The ratio is $780 / 190 \approx 4{,}1$.

questions.prompt: A dashboard keeps a list of sales sorted in ascending order by amount. For each new sale, it finds the right place in the already sorted list and shifts the following entries to the right. Which method illustrates this process?

options.text: Short-circuit evaluation: a second condition is sometimes skipped.
Insertion sort: insert new values at the appropriate position, one by one.
Aliasing: multiple variables point to the same array.
Call and return: a method returns its result.

questions.explanation: Insertion sort keeps a prefix sorted and inserts each new value at the appropriate position. The following entries are shifted to the right to make room.

questions.prompt: A gallery app creates a new `int[]` for 64 ratings. A loop copies each element exactly once into the new array. How many element assignments does the loop perform?
questions.explanation: Each of the 64 elements is assigned exactly once in the new array copy. That makes 64 assignments in total.

questions.prompt: In Java, you are checking whether a measurement exists at position `pos` and is nonnegative. With `&&`, the right-hand part is evaluated only if the left-hand part is true. Which condition checks the bounds before reading `samples[pos]`?

options.text: `pos < samples.length && samples[pos] >= 0`
`samples[pos] >= 0 && pos >= 0 && pos < samples.length`
`pos >= 0 && pos < samples.length && samples[pos] >= 0`
`samples[pos] >= 0`

questions.explanation: First, it checks whether `pos` is nonnegative and less than the array length. Due to short-circuit evaluation, `samples[pos]` is read only if both bounds checks are true.

questions.prompt: An app computes the total price with `int total = priceFor(cart);` and displays it afterward. What must happen before `total` contains the return value?

options.text: The app must sort `cart` first so that a return value is possible.
`priceFor` must directly change the local variable `total`.
`total` is automatically set to the final price before the call.
`priceFor` is called, computes the value, and returns with `return`.

questions.explanation: The synchronous call returns only after `priceFor` has computed and returned the value. The returned value is then assigned to `total` and can be displayed.
